name: First Time in the Twin Cities: Notes Toward Understanding
author: Amara Bergstrom-Okafor, cultural correspondent, The Laceworks Quarterly
description: A GLMZ cultural correspondent's first-person essay on arriving in the Twin Cities corridor for the first time, comparing two hundred years of divergent development.
body:
I expected it to feel like a smaller GLMZ. That was my mistake and it says more about my assumptions than about the Twin Cities.

I came in on the rail approach from the southeast, which gives you the Mississippi first and the city second. The river was a shock. I have lived my entire life with Lake Michigan as my water reference — vast, grey, increasingly strange. The Mississippi is something else: directional, purposeful, brown with carried soil, and the bridges across it are old in a way GLMZ's infrastructure is not old. Not ruined. Not maintained-into-uncanniness like the Canadian infrastructure. Old in the way that means people decided these were worth keeping and kept them. There are seven bridges visible from the rail approach and they span two hundred years of engineering philosophy and they all look like they belong together.

The first thing I noticed in the streets, which took me a full day to articulate: there is no tier system visible. I do not mean there is no inequality — there is, of course, there always is. I mean the spatial expression of it is different. In GLMZ, tier is altitude. It is literally inscribed in the vertical: the Gray Zone at ground level, the Spires above the clouds. In the Twin Cities, the gradations are horizontal. Wealthier districts blend into working districts blend into struggling districts across neighborhoods, not floors. You can walk from comfortable to difficult without taking an elevator. This feels, to a GLMZ resident, faintly dangerous and also somehow more honest.

The language is immediately noticeable. Standard GLMZ English is present — the rail station staff speak it, the commercial displays use it. But in the street and the markets and the places where people are not performing legibility for outsiders, there is something else. Linguists at Vellichor have written about Twin Cities Composite and I had read their papers, but reading about it and hearing it are different experiences. The Scandinavian substrate is audible — the prosody, the vowel length, certain constructions. But it is mixed with something I could only identify later as a preserved oral-performance tradition, the legacy of a spoken-word culture that apparently flourished here in the early twenty-first century and never quite stopped. People in the Twin Cities narrate. They tell the small stories of their days with a formal attention to structure — beginning, complication, resolution — that feels theatrical to my GLMZ ears and apparently feels perfectly normal to theirs.

They kept winter. This requires explanation. GLMZ has largely engineered around winter — climate control, covered walkways, the Gray Zone and Circuit are effectively year-round indoor environments. The Twin Cities has not done this. The city is built for winter: the skyway system connecting buildings is real and old and used, but the streets are also used, in February, by people who are dressed for it. There is a winter culture here that is not resigned to the season but genuinely organized around it. Ice fishing. Skating on the river in certain stretches that are not officially maintained for the purpose but where people skate anyway because they always have. A winter market on Nicollet that has been running every February since the early 2000s. The vendor stalls have lineages — this stall belongs to the granddaughter of the woman who ran it in 2180, who inherited it from her grandmother who ran it in 2080. They know this. They consider it worth knowing.

What I was least prepared for: how GLMZ is perceived from here. I mentioned where I was from at a dinner on my third evening and the table's response was politely complicated — the way you respond to someone who has mentioned they work for an entity that you have complicated feelings about. One woman, a transit planner whose name I should have written down, said something I have been thinking about since: 'We watch what happens in GLMZ the way you'd watch a river from high ground. We're glad you're doing what you're doing there. We chose not to.'

I do not think she was judging us. I think she was stating a fact. Two hundred years ago, both cities were midwestern, American, recognizable to each other. Whatever forces shaped GLMZ into what it is — the Consolidation, the corponations, the tier system, the sheer scale — those forces did not reach this far west. And the Twin Cities, left to itself, became something different. Not better. Not worse. Something that made different choices about what was worth keeping.

I flew back. On approach to GLMZ, the city rose out of the lake fog like a circuit board stood on its end — vertical, dense, brilliant with light. I have always found it beautiful. I still find it beautiful. I also, for the first time, found myself wondering what it looks like from the outside.
